title: Fats & Oils
subtitle: 600–1000 · Oil Retreats North, Tail Fat in Baghdad, the Tamil Chekku, the Tang Lamp and the First Northern Whalers

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Fights over stranded whales in Iceland

entries.label: Families fight over stranded whales in Iceland’s sagas
entries.hint: The Icelandic sagas, written down later but set in the settlement age, mention disputes between families over the ownership of whale carcasses — Ellis calls them ‘battles royal’ — which shows how much a stranded whale was worth. Vikings from Norway also brought to Iceland the technique of driving pilot whales into fjords. But Iceland had no active whale fishery as far as is known, and the Norse left no tryworks and no harpoons, so a whale-oil trade begins later.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis, Men and Whales (1991) pp.39–41 (PDF pp.63–64). The sagas postdate the events, so the date is the saga setting, not a record; the Norse silence on whaling is Ellis’s remark about the sources.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The Frankish estate rules for fat, butter and soap

entries.label: Emperor Temmu bans meat-eating in the farming months, 675
entries.hint: Japan’s first prohibition of meat eating, promulgated by Emperor Temmu in 675, banned indiscriminate fishing and hunting traps and forbade, from the fourth to the ninth months, the eating of beef, horse, dog, monkey and chicken, on pain of execution. It is usually read as Buddhist, though Ishige notes that it did not ban all meat and that it may have been prompted by fear for the already sparse number of animals. The whale, long thought of as a fish, stayed a permitted food. Japan had no systematic raising of livestock for meat or milk, so animal fat did not return as a cooking fat once the taboo took hold.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Ishige, The History and Culture of Japanese Food (2001), §§3.2–3.3, PDF pp.64–71 (the decree; the whale as fish; ‘the lack of dairy industry’). The last sentence is Ishige’s argument that the lack of herds, not the ideology alone, explains meat’s disappearance.

entries.label: The Capitulary De Villis: stewards must account for fat, tallow and soap
entries.hint: The extract of the Frankish capitulary on royal estates that circulates in English tells each steward to report to the lord at Christmas, among much else, on the honey and wax and ‘the fat, tallow, and soap’; to keep bacon, smoked meat, sausage, cheese, butter, beer, mead and wax ‘prepared and made with the greatest cleanliness’; to supply the women’s workrooms with soap and grease; to send two-thirds of the foods allowed on fast days, among them butter and cheese, to the lord; and to have soap makers and fishermen in his district. A northern estate economy run on animal fat, butter and soap.
entries.note: ANCHOR (translated extract read): Robinson (ed.), Readings in European History I (1904) pp.137–139, as posted on the Fordham Medieval Sourcebook (‘The Capitulary De Villis, 9th Century’); the page is an unnumbered extract, and search results date the whole text variously to the late 700s or early 800s, hence c.800. Lard and oil are not mentioned in the extract.

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Monastic oil in the north, the Prophet’s oil, and the lamps of the Tang monastery and the Chola temple

entries.label: Monasteries and cathedrals keep oil alive in a northern fat world
entries.hint: In the sea of barbarian beer, butter and lard, Mueller says, Christian monasteries and cathedrals remained islands of old-fashioned oil expertise: olive oil was needed for holy oils and church lamps and was a vital part of clerical diet; church councils decreed the protection of olive groves, sometimes forbidding the cutting of even a single tree; and monk-agronomists made oil by the advice of Cato and Columella read in their libraries.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history; no councils or dates given): Mueller, Extra Virginity (2011), the section after ‘Cookbooks, like histories, are written by the victors’. The ‘church councils’ are not named in the passage read, so the date is the folio’s span for the early medieval church, not an attested decree.

entries.label: The Prophet anoints himself with olive oil
entries.hint: Mueller writes that the Prophet Muhammad used so much olive oil on his skin that his shawl was often drenched with it, and that the three monotheistic religions that arose around the Mediterranean all filled their sacred texts with images of gnarled grey-green trees. The oil of the older religions passed into the new one’s ritual and diet as it did into its cooking (e2).
entries.note: UNVERIFIED (popular history; no hadith or source named): Mueller, Extra Virginity (2011), the opening chapter. The anecdote is repeated here as Mueller tells it; the hadith collections were not consulted.

entries.label: The ever-burning lamp in Tang monasteries
entries.hint: An oil lamp that in theory was never allowed to burn out, the changmingdeng, was a symbol in Chinese Buddhist monasteries, attested in Tang poems, ornate prose and the accounting records of the oil used for the lamp at a Dunhuang monastery. The seventh-century Chan monk Hongren used it as a symbol of the mind of correct enlightenment; more generally it was a perpetual offering to the Buddha.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Kieschnick, The Impact of Buddhism on Chinese Material Culture (2003), the section on monastic symbols (notes 229–230, citing Huang Zhaohan in Shijie zongjiao yanjiu 1987.1 on the lamp). The oil of the lamp is not specified in the passage read; Needham records sesame, perilla and other oils for lamps in the Sung (see fats-1000-1500).

entries.label: From milk to ghee: the Buddhist ladder in the Chinese pharmacopoeia
entries.hint: The Tang pharmacopoeia Hsin hsiu pen tshao (659), quoting Buddhist scripture, says that milk gives rise to lo (soured milk), lo to su, and su to ti hu, the clarified fat; the sequence of milk, lo, su and ti hu stands for the stages in the development of the soul, and the Shih liao pen tshao (670) and every later pharmacopoeia list the four. Ghee is the summit of the ladder, just as in Indian practice it was the offering of enormous prestige.
entries.note: SECONDARY (translation read in Needham): Needham, SCC 6.5 (2000) p.253 (PDF p.281), citing HHPT ch.15 p.171 and SLPT pp.29–30. The scripture quoted is not named in the passage; the parallel with the Indian prestige of ghee is the folio’s, see fats-1200bc-300bc::b1.

entries.label: Ninety sheep for a lamp: ghee endowments in the Chola country
entries.hint: Inscriptions of the reign of Parantaka I record gifts to temples for a perpetual lamp: typically a flock of 90 to 96 sheep (180 for two lamps) given by a village headman to supply the daily ghee, or a deposit of gold whose interest paid for a daily measure of oil (an ulakku) or for ghee on festival days. At Tiruvisalur, 180 sheep in year 16 (922–23) and 96 sheep in year 22 (928–29); at Tiruvidaimarudur, gold in years 18 and 19 (924–26) and 15 kalanju for 30 nali of ghee in year 36 (942–43). The lamp was fed by a herd.
entries.note: ANCHOR (inscriptions as transcribed): South Indian Inscriptions vol. 23 (Parantaka I), A.R. nos. 12, 31, 222, 238, 261 and 262 of 1907, as posted at whatisindia.com; the Gregorian years are the transcription’s conversion of regnal years. No study of the herd economy behind the gifts was read, so ‘fed by a herd’ is the folio’s summary of the gifts.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The Baghdad cookbook’s oven breads and frying fats

entries.label: Tang “foreign cakes”: fried in fragrant oil, sold on street corners by Iranians
entries.hint: Extremely popular in Tang times were the ‘foreign’ cakes, apparently fried or steamed breads brought from the West; a steamed variety containing sesame seeds was particularly well liked, and in the capital they were sold on street corners by foreign vendors, seemingly Iranians for the most part. Sesame, probably of Iranian origin, was known chiefly as a source of oil. A poem by Po Chü-i on sesame cakes has ‘the flour is light, the oil is fragrant’, clearly a fried cake; and a rice cake cooked in camel fat was sold as a cure for haemorrhoids.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read, OCR of a scanned copy): Schafer’s T’ang chapter in Chang (ed.) (1977), PDF pp.107, 127 and 148 (note 14, citing Po Chü-i in the Ch’üan T’ang shih). Compare fats-300bc-600ad::te2 and x2 for sesame’s arrival and the first pressing of seeds.

entries.label: Japan cooks without oil: sesame oil only for the nobility’s fried cakes
entries.hint: Ishige writes that virtually no cooking was done with oil or fat in traditional Japan: meat was not commonly eaten and butter was not produced, so cooking with animal fats was unknown. Sesame was cultivated and pressed, but the oil was very costly, and sesame was used mainly roasted as a seasoning. A rare recipe calling for sesame oil is the tōgashi, Chinese cakes of wheat, rice, soy or adzuki flour deep-fried in sesame oil and eaten as a dessert at the banquets of the nobility. Sautéing was a practice of Sung China, developed after Japan had suspended contact, and the absence of oil and fat became a distinctive trait of Japanese cooking: the arrival of Western and Chinese cooking in the late nineteenth century drew the reaction ‘so oily, so heavy’.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Ishige (2001), §3.6 ‘Cooking and banquet styles’, PDF pp.83–84. Ishige speaks of the ‘ancient age’ and the banquets of the Heian nobility (794–1185); the 800–1100 bracket is the folio’s.

entries.label: The Baghdad cookbook: tail fat in the pot, olive oil on the cold dishes
entries.hint: In Ibn Sayyar al-Warraq’s tenth-century cookbook, meat is first fried in rendered sheep’s tail fat (alya), a process called ‘sweating’ believed to remove bad odours; the tail fat was a delicacy across the Near East whatever the class, going back to ancient times, as the Babylonian recipes show. Cold dishes receive a generous drizzle of olive oil. When Arab dishes reached Christian Europe, bacon fat replaced the tail fat.
entries.note: ANCHOR (translation and introduction read): Nasrallah, Annals of the Caliphs’ Kitchens (2007), Introduction (PDF pp.36, 41, 56, 60) — tabrīq, the esteemed alya, olive oil on cold dishes; the Latin Liber de coquina (13th century) as the first European mention of the dishes, with bacon fat in place of tail fat. The date follows the Sugar folio (sugar-600-1000::e2). See also fats-8000bc-1200bc::e1 for the same fat in the Babylonian tablets.

entries.label: Oil on the oven wall: sesame or unripe-olive oil in Baghdad’s bread
entries.hint: The cookbook’s bread recipes rub each dough piece with a teaspoon of sesame oil or of zayt anfāq, oil from unripe olives, before sticking it to the smouldering oven wall, and pour pure olive oil or sesame oil into bottles for bottle-bread batter. Clarified butter enriches the sweets (a yeast cake is drenched in fresh milk, clarified butter and sugar) and the travellers’ flour sawīq, mixed with a measure of goat’s and cow’s clarified butter, while the tail fat of e1 does the frying.
entries.note: ANCHOR (translation read): Nasrallah (2007) PDF pp.56, 132–133, 140 (the sweets, the oven breads and the sawīq recipes); a footnote on PDF p.174 explains that dasam is the grease of meat and fat, and duhn the word for fats and oils such as butter and sesame oil.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Arabic oil words in Spanish and the Baghdad dietetics of fat

entries.label: Spanish takes its oil words from Arabic: aceite and aceituna
entries.hint: Spanish aceite (oil) comes from Andalusi Arabic az-zayt, from Arabic zayt, and aceituna (olive) from az-zaytūna. The words show that the language of oil in Iberia was reshaped under Muslim rule, even though olive growing in Spain is far older (see fats-1200bc-300bc::x1). They do not show that the Arabs introduced the crop: Squatriti, reviewing Andrew Watson’s ‘Arab agricultural revolution’, notes that classicists object to crediting the early caliphate with plants that the ancients already grew.
entries.note: SECONDARY (linguistic; popular language pages found by web search, no dictionary read): the derivations. Squatriti, ‘Of Seeds, Seasons, and Seas: Andrew Watson’s Medieval Agrarian Revolution Forty Years Later’, Journal of Economic History 74 (2014) pp.1205–1220 (PDF p.6) — the passage on the dispute concerns durum wheat and artichokes and does not mention olives, so the olive point is the folio’s application of it.

entries.label: Butter ‘floats at the stomach’s mouth’: the Baghdad cookbook on fat and the body
entries.hint: The tenth-century Baghdad cookbook judges fats by their effect on the humours: fried fatty meat is hard and slow to digest, though frying in olive oil makes it lighter; butter is not easy to digest because it floats near the top opening of the stomach, but clarified butter (samn) slackens the stomach, relaxes stiffness and helps in snakebite and hot-wind cases, while overindulgence triggers phlegmatic diseases.
entries.note: ANCHOR (translation read): Nasrallah, Annals of the Caliphs’ Kitchens (2007) the chapters on the humoral properties of foods, PDF pp.121 and 145. The dietetic sections are the cookbook’s own and may be drawn from earlier medical writers; the translator does not say which.

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Anglo-Saxon and Irish butter, the Tamil press, Italian soap, northern whaling, Japan’s so and Africa’s shea

entries.label: Abu Mansur lists sesame as a crop of Iran
entries.hint: In their account of sesame in Iran, Mortazavian and Kohpayegani note that Abu Mansur, writing in the late tenth century in his Al-abnieh an Haghaegh-ol-Advieh, mentions sesame as a crop plant in Iran. They add that Ershad-o-Zerat describes sesame cultivation in ancient Iran, without dating it.
entries.note: CONTEXT (book read, second hand): Mortazavian & Kohpayegani, ‘Sesame Cultivation and Use in Iran’, in Bedigian, ed., Sesame: The Genus Sesamum (2011), PDF p.346 (printed p.321). Only the mention is reported, with no passage or place; the book’s title is given in the chapter’s own transliteration. Compare e1 and e2 for the Baghdad cookbook’s sesame oil.

entries.label: Coyol, huiscoyol and cohune: the Maya’s own answer to a lean, fat-poor diet
entries.date: c.AD 400–800 (Classic period; Cerén’s eruption securely dated c.AD 600)
entries.loc: Copán, Honduras, and Cerén, El Salvador
entries.hint: The Maya domesticated turkeys, Muscovy ducks and dogs, but most of their animal meat still came from white-tailed deer — a lean meat by any reckoning — and plant fat sources were otherwise limited to a short list (mamey, squash seed, avocado). Into that gap came three native palms, all recovered archaeobotanically across the region: coyol, huiscoyol and cohune, all good oil producers. At Copán the evidence suggests the Maya did not just gather coyol in the wild but actually cultivated it, introducing the palm to the region — “the Copán Maya recognized the value of the palm and cultivated it to enhance their nutritional options,” in the excavator’s own words. Oddly, the otherwise exceptionally well-preserved village of Cerén, buried whole by a volcanic eruption, shows no extensive use of palms at all; the excavator can only guess that Cerén got its fat some other way. After the Spanish conquest, the whole picture changed again: the old plant-based fat economy gave way within a few generations to the fat of Old World domesticated animals.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): David L. Lentz, ‘Plant Resources of the Ancient Maya: The Paleoethnobotanical Evidence’, ch.1 in Christine D. White (ed.), Reconstructing Ancient Maya Diet (University of Utah Press, 1999), PDF pp.37–38, drawing on the author’s own fieldwork (Lentz 1990, 1991a, 1993; Lentz et al. 1996) at Copán and Cerén. The coyol-cultivation claim rests on Lentz’s own citation of Smith (1967) and his own 1991a paper, not read directly here. The same chapter notes, separately and more speculatively, that small quantities of cottonseed oil could in theory have been used for cooking without a toxic gossypol dose — a calculation, not a find, so not used as its own claim here. Compare th6 and te5 for the folio’s broader argument that fat was structurally scarce across the pre-Columbian Americas; this is the clearest documented exception to that rule found in this program so far. Compare fats-1500-1750::ec18 for the post-conquest pig that, in Lentz’s own words, supplied the fat that followed.

entries.label: Butter is a luxury in Anglo-Saxon England
entries.hint: In Anglo-Saxon territories butter was typically made from sheep’s milk, a remnant of Roman occupation: cows were kept to breed the plough oxen, while sheep supplied wool, tallow, milk and meat. Butter was a minor by-product of cheese from ewe’s milk — about two pounds for every hundred pounds of cheese — so only the nobility or the local thane enjoyed it. Only in the High Middle Ages, as wool and milk separated, did dairying shift to cattle and butter become affordable.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history): Khosrova, Butter: A Rich History (2016) ch.1 pp.35–36 (PDF pp.56–57). No source is given for the butter-to-cheese ratio in the pages read.

entries.label: The Tamil chekku: sesame oil pressed and exported
entries.hint: The Tamil texts Nāladiyār and Nālāyira Divya Prabandham of the 7th and 8th centuries describe the sesame oil press, the chekku, and the foam (nurai) noted in the much earlier Puranānūru suggests the press was in use even then. Sesame oil was exported from the south, as coconut oil was in the 1st century.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Tamil not read): Achaya, Indian Food Tradition (1994) p.47 (PDF p.65, OCR of a scanned PDF). The inference from the foam to an older press is Achaya’s.

entries.label: Shea butter at Kirikongo: a 1,400-year record from Burkina Faso
entries.hint: Excavations at Kirikongo, a village site in western Burkina Faso, found thousands of charred shea-nut fragments in households built on top of one another; the sequence, running from about 100 AD to 1500 AD, was in 2016 the longest continuous single-site record of shea use known, and the thickness of the nutshells shows that different households drew on different tree populations and managed shea trees within their fields. A 2024 follow-up on the charcoal reads the rise and fall of shea wood as the growth and later shrinking of a shea parkland. The folio files the whole record under these centuries.
entries.note: SECONDARY (abstracts and a press release found by web search; the paper itself not read — the publisher page returned no text): Gallagher, Dueppen & Walsh, ‘The Archaeology of Shea Parklands (Vitellaria paradoxa) in Burkina Faso’, Journal of Ethnobiology 36(1) 2016 (DOI 10.2993/0278-0771-36.1.150); Höhn, Dueppen, Gallagher & Lammers, Journal of Global Archaeology 2024. The site is not the earliest shea use in West Africa, only the longest continuous sequence known to 2016.

entries.label: Pannage: pigs fed on the autumn mast of the forest
entries.hint: For most of their domesticated history, Gade writes in Kiple, pigs were kept either free-ranging in forests or sedentary in settlements. In Western Europe, where domestic pigs have been known since before 4000 BC, range pigs ate acorns, chestnuts, beechnuts, hazelnuts and wild fruit, and dug mushrooms, roots, worms and grubs out of the ground. Pannage, pasturing pigs in a forest, was recorded from antiquity. In the early Middle Ages mast rights were a greater source of income from the forest than the sale of wood, peasants had to fence their fields against the pigs, and the pannage season was fixed by seigneurial decree: in many places mast feeding began on the feast of Saint Michael, 29 September, and ended on the last day of November. Mast feeding has now disappeared from Europe except in a few places, best known in Spain, where black and red Iberian swine still feed in the oak woods and make the cured hams of Jabugo.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read): Gade, ‘Hogs (Pigs)’, in Kiple & Ornelas, eds., The Cambridge World History of Food (2000), PDF pp.574–575 (printed pp.537–538), citing Laurans (1976) for the Saint Michael dates. The passage is about pig-keeping and forest income, and does not name lard or fat; the bracket 600–1000 stands for the ‘early Middle Ages’ of the source. Compare o1 for the estates’ bacon, fat and soap.

entries.label: Birnirk hunters on the Bering Strait: seals, lamps and a disputed whale hunt
entries.loc: The Alaska North Slope and the Chukchi Peninsula
entries.hint: The Birnirk culture, descended from the Old Bering Sea and Okvik traditions, appears first on the American side of the Bering Strait and spreads to the Chukchi Peninsula; genetic evidence shows its people are the direct ancestors of the Thule. Birnirk houses had no open fireplace: heat and light came from stone and clay lamps, of the same general kind that elsewhere in the Arctic burned seal or whale oil, though the sources read here do not name Birnirk’s own fuel. The people hunted seals, caribou, birds and fish with distinctive harpoons; a whaling harpoon and whale-part artefacts (baleen, whale bone) at Utqiagvik suggest some hunting of whales, but one source cautions that organised whaling usually needs more crew than Birnirk’s small settlements had, so how much whale they actually took is disputed.
entries.note: SECONDARY (Wikipedia article read, 24 October 2026 revision, itself citing Gibbon & Ames, Archaeology of Prehistoric Native America (1998) pp.72–73 for the dates and subsistence picture; Sturtevant, ed., Handbook of North American Indians vol. 5: Arctic (1985) p.91 for lamps and tools; the National Park Service’s Birnirk National Historic Landmark page for the site; and Raghavan et al., ‘The genetic prehistory of the New World Arctic’, Science 345 (2014), for the Thule-ancestry finding). None of the underlying sources were read directly. The lamp fuel is the folio’s inference from the wider Arctic lamp tradition (compare fats-1200bc-300bc::te6), not stated for Birnirk itself; the whaling is flagged CONTESTED in the source it names.

entries.label: Dairy fats reach their peak in China under the part-Turkic Tang
entries.hint: Anderson writes that in medieval China, as Buddhism turned people away from beef, cream, yogurt, kumiss, cheese, curds and butter were popular; since the Tang dynasty’s own family was of part-Turkic background, these foods took on status, and this seems to have been the climax of dairy consumption in China. Ishige adds that outside the north dairy was an extremely rare luxury or medicine for the Han upper class until the Ming, and that China milked north of the Great Wall but not generally to the south.
entries.note: ANCHOR (books read): Anderson, The Food of China (1988), the chapter on medieval China, PDF p.66; Ishige (2001) §3.3, PDF pp.69–71. Compare fats-300bc-600ad::te4 for the sixth-century manual that teaches churning su.

entries.label: Tang kaymak and ti-hu: the dairy fats of the banquet
entries.hint: In Tang China the pharmacologists argued whether cow or goat kaymak, clotted cream, was better; the poet Pi Jih-hsiu rated a lavish feast dish as flavoursome as kaymak, and it was used in the finest pastries, one banquet menu naming kaymak mixed with honey. Ti-hu, similar to the ghee of India, was thought more refined than kaymak as one Buddhist sutra was more refined than another, was used in the most exquisite dishes, and was prescribed by Sun Ssu-mo as a tonic for bones and marrow; a poet put clarified butter mixed into fine wine in a Buddhist monastery.
entries.note: ANCHOR (book read, OCR of a scanned copy): Edward Schafer’s chapter on the T’ang in Chang (ed.), Food in Chinese Culture (1977) p.107 (PDF p.116). Compare fats-600-1000::b3 for the Buddhist ladder from milk to ti-hu and ec8 for the Tang dairy peak.

entries.label: Japan’s court makes so, a milk-skin dairy product, and takes it as tribute
entries.hint: Between the 7th and 10th centuries Japan made a dairy product called so, produced by solidifying layers of milk skin; it is first recorded in the reign of Mommu (697–707), the Ministry of the Imperial Household’s office made it, it served as medicine and as an offering to the gods, and it was given in kind to the emperors, with Ajifu in Settsu a known production site. The Engishiki of 927 lists an overseer of milk, and a Japanese paper dates a tribute system to 887. A popular article ties the end of this dairy economy to the collapse of aristocratic power late in the Heian period.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Wikipedia ‘So (dairy product)’ (read, citing the Japan Dairy Industry Association’s history page); the Engishiki overseer and the 887 tribute date are from web-search summaries of a Kansai University paper and a China Story article, not read in full. Compare fats-600-1000::b3 for the Chinese ladder from milk to su.

entries.label: Butter buried in the Irish bogs
entries.hint: Hundreds of batches of buried ‘bog butter’ have been found in Irish peat, wrapped in moss in wooden firkins or tubes or animal bladders, some from as early as 400 BC. A pail more than a thousand years old in the Cork Butter Museum was made when Ireland was emerging from tribal wars and Viking conquests; hiding it in the bog may have been protection from raiders, or a way to keep it cool and sealed through the warm months.
entries.note: SECONDARY (popular history): Khosrova (2016) pp.24–26 and p.47 (PDF pp.45–46, 68). The one-thousand-year age is the museum label as Khosrova reports it; the explanations (hiding from invaders, preservation) are the author’s and are not tested.

entries.label: Soap becomes a craft, above all in Italy
entries.hint: Soap making was a well-established craft in the early Middle Ages, a sign that by then soap was being made on an industrial basis, particularly on the Italian peninsula. Tallow was the main fat in northern Europe, olive oil in the Mediterranean; wool washing, before spinning, was a large part of the demand.
entries.note: SECONDARY: Ward, The Clean Body: A Modern History (2019), section ‘The art of soap making’ (early Middle Ages; Italy; tallow in the north and olive oil in the Mediterranean; by the early 17th century England and France lead, centred on London and Marseille). The date is the folio’s span for ‘the early Middle Ages’, which Ward does not narrow.

entries.label: Ohthere hunts whales and walrus; whaling in the North Sea by the 800s
entries.loc: The White Sea and the North Sea
entries.hint: In King Alfred’s translation of Orosius, about 890, the Norwegian Ohthere describes the whale- and walrus-hunting of a northern people on the White Sea. The Belgian historian De Smet finds whaling in the North Sea and English Channel certainly from the 800s onward, on the evidence of the regularity with which whale meat appears in markets, and Norse whalers may have taught the Basques. There is no evidence that this was a regular commercial fishery.
entries.note: SECONDARY (scholarly summary): Ellis, Men and Whales (1991) pp.38–40 and 44 (PDF pp.62, 67), quoting Jenkins 1921 and De Smet. The large ‘whales’ Ohthere hunted may be walrus and bowhead; the oil is not mentioned in the passage read.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: Pressing seeds for oil in Tang China

entries.label: Pressing seeds for oil is a Tang farming task
entries.hint: The late-Tang calendar of farm work Ssu shih tsuan yao lists pressing seeds for oil among the jobs for the fourth month of the year. Vegetable oils, already a significant part of the Chinese economy in the 500s, probably kept expanding under the Tang, and by the Sung they were a major traded commodity.
entries.note: SECONDARY (translation read in Needham): Needham, SCC 6.5 (2000) p.440 (PDF p.468) — the Ssu shih tsuan yao (late Tang) and Needham’s ‘probably continued to expand during the Thang’. The passage gives no description of the press.
